branches.name: left (city) branch around the Tiber Island
branches.note: Pons Fabricius (62 BC, c. 62 m long) spans it; still essentially the ancient width. The centerline above follows the right branch.

branches.name: right (Trastevere) branch around the Tiber Island
branches.note: Widened to 70 m in 1888-92, when the Pons Cestius was rebuilt longer; the ancient bridge was c. 48.5 m long, so the ancient Trastevere bank stood c. 20 m further into today's channel.

tiber.waterLevelUnits: m asl at the Tiber Island, normal (non-flood) stage, imperial period

waterLevelByYear.t: 6th c. BC: dry-season depth 2 m or less over a channel floor at c. -1 m (Brock et al.)
Cloaca Maxima outlet sill at 4.7 m sits just above normal water
Trajanic Emporium quays: c. 5 m sloping wall up to a travertine quay at c. 11 m
1822-1921 mean 6.7 on the Ripetta gauge (zero c. 1 m asl, but Aldrete treats readings as m asl)

tiber.waterLevelProfileNote: Add these offsets (m) to waterLevelByYear along the centerline indices: the normal-stage slope through the city is c. 0.13-0.2 m/km.
tiber.bedNote: Channel floor c. 0 to -1 m asl in the 6th c. BC (Brock et al.) and roughly the same today; Aldrete notes suggestions that the Roman bed was 0.5-1 m lower than now.

floodStages.t: minor flood: Forum Boarium, Emporium and the riverside Campus Martius under water (Augustan topography)
major flood: whole Campus Martius to the foot of the Pincian and Quirinal, Transtiberim to the Janiculum, Circus Maximus valley; Forum floods by backflow through the Cloaca

embankments.note: Canevari's muraglioni: walls 100 m apart at the base and 110 m at the top, crest 18.45 m on the Ripetta gauge (c. 19.4 asl), 8 m low quays (banchine); island branches fixed at 60 m (left) and 70 m (right). The regularization widened the bed in some stretches and narrowed it in others; the Porto di Ripetta was buried and the Ripa Grande port demolished.

outlets.name: Cloaca Maxima
outlets.note: Outlet visible in the modern embankment below the Round Temple (Ponte Palatino); sill at 4.7 m asl. The open archaic channel (Spinon) entered the river at about the same point.

outlets.name: Cloaca of the Circus Maximus (Nodinus / Aqua Crabra outfall)
outlets.note: About 100 m downstream of the Cloaca Maxima; mouth still visible (Platner, Circus Maximus).

outlets.name: Petronia Amnis (option A: into the river a little above the Ponte Garibaldi, opposite the island)
outlets.note: Hülsen-Jordan / Lanciani course: from the E end of the Porticus of Pompey south through the later Ghetto.

outlets.name: Petronia Amnis (option B: under the Porticus of Pompey to the Navalia)
Euripus (outflow of the Stagnum Agrippae)
outlets.note: Exact line unknown; usually drawn W along Corso Vittorio Emanuele to the river near the Ponte Vittorio Emanuele.

segments.name: Pons Milvius to the Campus Martius (Ager Vaticanus / Via Flaminia)
segments.note: Unconfined, wider and shallower channel with gravel bars; ancient banks taken c. 10-15 m outside today's water edges. Modern Lungotevere Flaminio / Prati walls are on fill (corrections 'lungotevere_*').

segments.name: N Campus Martius (Mausoleum of Augustus, later Porto di Ripetta)
segments.note: The left bank lay roughly at the modern wall foot; the Hadrianic dike across the N Campus stood back from the water. Porto di Ripetta (1704) buried under the Lungotevere in Augusta.

segments.name: Campus bend at the Pons Aelius and Pons Neronianus (Tarentum)
segments.note: Outer bend; the Tarentum lay on the inner (left) side. The 1880s works trimmed the bend; ancient left bank c. 5-15 m inland of the modern wall foot.

segments.name: Via Giulia reach (Trigarium, Navalia?, Pons Agrippae)
segments.note: Cippi of the Augustan and Tiberian curatores riparum mark the public strip along the bank; houses backed onto the river until 1880.

segments.name: Tiber Island
segments.note: Island 269 x 67 m (Platner); the OSM islet also includes a long modern upstream spur toward the Ponte Garibaldi, clipped off here, and the outline is shrunk 8 m to remove the 1880s-90s quays; ship-shaped travertine revetment at the SE end. Left branch c. 55 m (Pons Fabricius), right branch c. 48 m (Pons Cestius before 1888-92).

segments.name: Forum Boarium / Portus Tiberinus (Pons Aemilius, Pons Sublicius)
segments.note: In the 6th c. BC the left bank stood c. 100 m E of the modern course (see archaicLeftBank); the river shifted W and silted up during the 6th-3rd c. BC. Late-Republican embankments under the Temple of Portunus and the Round Temple fix the bank near the modern wall, where the Cloaca outlet still opens.

segments.name: Under the Aventine cliff (Porta Trigemina, Salinae)
Emporium (Lungotevere Testaccio)
segments.note: Quays of 193/174 BC rebuilt under Claudius and Trajan run c. 500 m along Lungotevere Testaccio; parts are incorporated in the modern embankment, so the ancient quay front lies at the foot of the modern wall.

segments.name: S of the Aurelian Wall (Pietra Papa wharves, Via Ostiensis)
segments.note: Wide shallow reach with wharves for c. 2 km downstream.

archaicLeftBank.note: Brock et al.: 6th c. BC bank about 100 m E of the modern course, just below the Capitoline ledge at Sant'Omobono (6-7.4 m) and a low shore near the Aventine (c. 1 m). Fill and silt pushed the bank W by c. 100 m over a front of c. 300 m before the 3rd c. BC.

tarentum.note: See waters 'tarentum'. In extremo Martio campo where the Tiber bends; hot springs and vapours.

tiber.notes: Centerline: OpenStreetMap waterway 'Tevere' resampled to 130 points (c. 110 m spacing) from lat 41.937 to 41.848. 'width' is the reconstructed ancient water-surface width at normal stage (m), 'widthModernWater' the modern low-water width between the 8 m quays measured from the OSM water polygons. ancientBanks are the centreline offset along local normals by the ancient half-widths (left = city/east side looking downstream). Through the island reach the centreline follows the right branch; the left branch is in 'branches'. The modern DEM inside the channel is unusable (DSM with plane-tree canopy over the water, reading 10-30 m): cut the channel from these data. Normal level rose through antiquity as the bed aggraded: about 1-2 m asl in the 6th c. BC, 4-5 m in the late Republic and Empire, 5-7 m in the 19th-20th c. (Aldrete's 5-7 m is the modern gauge record projected back).

sources.r: 2.5.2-4 (origin of the island); 35.21.5 (flood of 193 BC carries away two bridges)

scholarship: Aldrete, Floods of the Tiber in Ancient Rome (2007) 40-48, 72-90, 193-196, 247-250
Brock, Motta and Terrenato, 'On the banks of the Tiber: opportunity and transformation in early Rome', JRS 111 (2021)
Brock, 'Envisioning Rome's prehistoric river harbor: an update from the Sant'Omobono coring project', Antiquity (2017) / east bank of the Tiber below the island
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) 281-282 (Insula Tiberina), 536-538 (Tiberis)
Le Gall, Il Tevere, fiume di Roma nell'antichità (2005)
Mocchegiani Carpano, 'Il Tevere: archeologia e commercio', BNum 2-3 (1984) 21-81
isolatiberina.org, I muraglioni del Tevere (branch widths 60/70 m)
Frosini, Il Tevere: le inondazioni di Roma (1977)

waters.name: Velabrum (seasonal marsh and flood basin)

floodedAfter.note: After the Cloaca Maxima the area dried but floods up to c. 10 m kept covering it until the late Republic.

scholarship: Ammerman, 'Environmental archaeology in the Velabrum, Rome: interim report', JRA 11 (1998) 213-223 (wet in winter, dry in summer; not a permanent swamp)
Aldrete, Floods of the Tiber in Ancient Rome (2007) 168-169
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) (Velabrum)
waters.note: Low ground between the Palatine and Capitoline connecting the Forum valley to the Forum Boarium; natural surface 4-7 m. Drawn as a shallow seasonal water body; the engine may show it full in winter years and as wet meadow otherwise.

waters.name: Forum valley marsh (before the landfill and Cloaca)

sources.r: 6.401-402 (hic, ubi nunc fora sunt, udae tenuere paludes)

scholarship: Ammerman, 'On the origins of the Forum Romanum', AJA 94 (1990) 627-645 (natural floor c. 6-7 m; landfill of at least 10,000 m3 raises it to c. 9 m at the end of the 7th c. BC)
Aldrete, Floods of the Tiber in Ancient Rome (2007) 177
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) 230 (the centre of the valley originally a swamp)
waters.note: Ammerman argues the Forum was a seasonally flooded basin rather than a permanent lake; the polygon covers the lowest part around the later Lacus Curtius.

waters.name: Spinon (Forum stream, later canalised as the Cloaca Maxima)

becomes.note: open canal under the Tarquins, vaulted in stages (2nd-1st c. BC); still functioning

sources.r: 3.52 (Spino among the streams in the augurs' prayer)

scholarship: Lanciani, The Ruins and Excavations of Ancient Rome (1897) 29 (Spinon drained the basin between Quirinal and Esquiline: Vicus Longus, Vicus Patricius, Subura, Argiletum, Forum, Velabrum, to the mouth of the Cloaca Maxima)
LTUR IV s.v. Spino (H. Bauer)
Hopkins, The Cloaca Maxima and the monumental manipulation of water in archaic Rome (2007)
waters.note: Name and course follow Lanciani; others apply 'Spinon' to the stream between Quirinal and Pincian. Upper tributaries from the Vicus Longus and Vicus Patricius join at the Subura.

waters.name: Nodinus (stream of the Labicana valley and Vallis Murcia)

becomes.note: covered when the spina was made permanent; the cloaca still drains the valley (now the Acqua Mariana collector)

scholarship: Lanciani, The Ruins and Excavations of Ancient Rome (1897) 29 (Nodinus, 3600 m long, with eight tributaries from the springs of Apollo, the Camenae, Mercury, the Piscina Publica; into the Tiber a little below the Cloaca Maxima)

Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) 114 (stream of the Circus from the valley between Caelian and Esquiline, through Nero's later stagnum, into the Tiber c. 100 m below the Cloaca Maxima)
LTUR III s.v. Nodinus (L. Anselmino)
Funiciello et al., 'Geology of the Colosseum valley', Annali di Geofisica 38 (1995) 927-937 (valley floor levelled to c. 14 m asl by Holocene alluvium; present ground c. 22 m)
waters.note: Lanciani's identification. Rises E of the Colosseum (Fosso Labicano), flows past the Meta Sudans, S along the Via di S. Gregorio to Porta Capena, where the Aqua Crabra joins, then along the axis of the Vallis Murcia.

waters.name: Aqua Crabra (Marrana; later Marrana Mariana)
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) (Aqua Crabra)
Calixtus II's Marrana Mariana (1122) reused the course through Porta Metronia
waters.note: Natural stream from the Alban slopes (Tusculum) through the Vallis Camenarum, entering the Aurelian circuit at Porta Metronia and joining the Nodinus at Porta Capena. Partly channelled; mills used it in the Middle Ages.

waters.name: Lacus Curtius

monumentAfter.note: paved enclosure with a puteal (C. Curtius, cos. 445 BC); dry under Augustus ('siccas ... aras', Ovid)

scholarship: Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) 310-311
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
waters.note: The last pool of the Forum marsh in the tradition; small polygon at the monument's site in the centre of the Forum.

waters.name: Lacus Iuturnae (spring of Juturna)
scholarship: Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) 311-313 (basin 2.12 m deep, 5.13 x 5.04 m, older tufa pavement at 10.90 m)
waters.note: Spring at the foot of the Palatine by the Temple of Castor, where the Dioscuri watered their horses after Lake Regillus. Basin form from the late Republic / Tiberius; the spring flowed earlier.

waters.name: Tullianum spring (lower chamber of the Carcer)
scholarship: Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) 99-100 (a small spring still rises in the floor; Tullianum perhaps from tullus, spring)
Lanciani, The Ruins and Excavations of Ancient Rome (1897) 233
waters.note: Elevation estimated from the Forum levels (the chamber floor lies c. 12 Roman feet below the upper room).

waters.name: Fons Camenarum (spring and grove of the Camenae)
scholarship: Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) (Camenae, outside the Porta Capena)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
waters.note: Vestals drew water here daily; placed in the valley just outside the Porta Capena at the foot of the Caelian (Villa Celimontana).

waters.name: Fons Mercurii (near the Porta Capena)
scholarship: Lanciani, The Ruins and Excavations of Ancient Rome (1897) 29
waters.note: One of the Nodinus tributaries named by Lanciani.

waters.name: Cati fons (source of the Petronia)

alternatives.note: Coarelli: on the collis Mucialis near Via XXIV Maggio / Via Mazzarino, feeding the Lacus Fundani

scholarship: Digital Augustan Rome, s.v. Cati Fons
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) 389
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
waters.note: Traditionally the Acqua di S. Felice in the courtyard of the Quirinal Palace (Via della Panetteria), on the W flank near the Porta Salutaris.

waters.name: Petronia Amnis

becomes.note: channelled underground as the Campus was built over; the auspicia peremnia were still taken at its crossing

sources.r: 250 M (Petronia amnis est in Tiberim perfluens, quam magistratus auspicato transeunt)

scholarship: Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) 389 (SW across Piazza Venezia, W to the E end of the Porticus of Pompey, then S to the river opposite the island or W to the Navalia)
Lanciani, The Ruins and Excavations of Ancient Rome (1897) 29 (collected the Sallustian springs and fell into the Tiber a little above the Ponte Garibaldi)
waters.note: Boundary of the urban auspices. Main line = southern course (Hülsen-Jordan, Lanciani); lineAlt = western course to the Navalia (AR 1909). Lanciani also derives it from the Sallustian springs; that branch is 'aqua_sallustiana'.

waters.name: Aqua Sallustiana (stream of the Vallis Sallustiana; 'Spinon' in some reconstructions)
scholarship: Lanciani, The Ruins and Excavations of Ancient Rome (1897) 29 (Petronia collected the Sallustian springs; nymphaeum over them in Piazza Sallustiana)
romanoimpero.com, Le sorgenti di Roma (Venuti on the subterranean Sallustian water under Via del Tritone, S. Claudio)
waters.note: Valley of the Horti Sallustiani, Piazza Barberini and Via del Tritone, flowing into the Palus Caprae; the subsoil there is still saturated (Acqua Sallustiana). Aldrete's map shows 10-15 m of fill along Via del Tritone.

waters.name: Palus Caprae (Goat's Marsh)
scholarship: Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) 92 (the largest swamp, where were afterwards the pool and baths of Agrippa)
Aldrete, Floods of the Tiber in Ancient Rome (2007) 46 (Augustan-era remnant floods at 10 m)
Digital Augustan Rome, s.v. Campus Martius
waters.note: Central Campus Martius W of the later Pantheon. Polygon conjectural; Agrippa converted it into the Stagnum and Baths.

waters.name: Stagnum Agrippae
scholarship: Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) 518-520 (W of the Thermae, N of Corso Vittorio Emanuele, between Via di Monterone and Via dei Sediari)
Haselberger et al., Mapping Augustan Rome (JRA Suppl. 50, 2002)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
waters.note: Size and end date unknown; c. 200 x 105 m adopted, long axis E-W. It probably silted up or was built over in late antiquity.

waters.name: Euripus (canal from the Stagnum Agrippae to the Tiber)
scholarship: Haselberger et al., Mapping Augustan Rome (JRA Suppl. 50, 2002)
Digital Augustan Rome, s.v. Euripus
waters.note: Artificial watercourse across the W Campus; line schematic.

waters.name: Tarentum (hot springs and vapours by the Tiber bend)

sources.r: 2.4.5 (altar of Dis found 20 feet below ground)

scholarship: Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) 508-509 (altar discovered 1888 between the Chiesa Nuova and Piazza Sforza Cesarini)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
waters.note: Not a water body proper but a volcanic spot (hot springs and smoke) believed an entrance to the underworld; marked so the engine can show steam/marsh texture. Point placed between the Chiesa Nuova and Piazza Sforza Cesarini where the altar was found (the Wikidata point, 12.46505 41.90023, falls on the Lungotevere at the water's edge).

waters.name: Stagnum of Nero's Domus Aurea (lake in the Colosseum valley)

sources.r: 31.1 (stagnum maris instar, circumsaeptum aedificiis ad urbium speciem)

scholarship: Funiciello et al., 'Geology of the Colosseum valley', Annali di Geofisica 38 (1995) 927-937 (valley floor levelled to c. 14 m asl by Holocene alluvium; present ground c. 22 m)
Lancaster, 'The Colosseum: construction' (drain of the 6th c. BC near the Arch of Constantine at c. 11 m asl; foundations at 8-9 m asl)
Hopkins and Beard, The Colosseum (2005) (spoil raised the ground almost 7 m above c. 4 m of Neronian fire debris)
Panella, Meta Sudans I (1996)
waters.note: Begun after the fire of July 64, drained for the Colosseum (begun c. 70-72). Extent schematic: the amphitheatre (188 x 156 m) is usually said to occupy the lake's site; it may have been a formal rectangular basin.

waters.name: Naumachia Augusti (Transtiberim)

sources.r: 23 (1800 x 1200 feet, 30 beaked ships and more small ones, 3000 men)

scholarship: Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) (Naumachia Augusti; island in the centre, pons naumachiarius)
Taylor, 'Torrent or trickle? The Aqua Alsietina, the Naumachia Augusti and the Transtiberim', AJA 101 (1997) 465-492
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
waters.note: 1800 x 1200 Roman feet = 533 x 355 m. Located around S. Cosimato (Wikidata point 12.4708, 41.8867); orientation unknown, long axis set parallel to the Janiculum foot (bearing 160). Used by Titus (AD 80) and perhaps restored by Philip in 247; Dio says parts remained in his day.

waters.name: Naumachia Vaticana (so-called; near Castel Sant'Angelo)
scholarship: Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) (Naumachiae: one perhaps the naumachia Augusti, the other the so-called naumachia Vaticana)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) (Naumachia Traiani)
waters.note: Remains of a large basin found in Prati in the 1740s and 1880s are often identified as Trajan's naumachia (Naumachia Traiani, dedicated 109) and listed by the Regionaries in Region XIV. Size and dates conjectural; included so the engine can switch it off.
